background.definition: Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (previously known as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia; PCP) is a pneumonia arising in immunosuppressed persons. Prior to 1981, most of the cases occurred in patients with malignancy. Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia will be referred to as PCP henceforth.

list.listitem: Incidence of PCP is declining as more patients receive PCP prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy (ART).
Recent incidence rates among patients with AIDS in Western Europe and US are <1 case per 100 person years.
PCP was a major cause of death in patients with AIDS prior to widespread PCP prophylaxis and ART.
The diagnosis of PCP should be considered more frequently in immunocompromised patients without HIV, because prompt diagnosis may improve the prognosis for these patients.

Overall mortality of PCP in patients who do not have AIDS may be as high as 30% to 50%. The primary underlying conditions in patients without HIV with PCP are hematological malignancies (32.5%), solid tumors (18.2%), inflammatory diseases (14.9%), solid organ transplant (12.3%), and vasculitis (9.7%).

In kidney transplant patients, the following were found in a systemic review and meta-anlysis to be risk factors for PCP: age greater than 50 years old, CMV infection, BK viremia, acute rejection, ABO-incompatibility, decreased eGFR and lymphopenia .
The organism that causes PCP is Pneumocystis jiroveci.
It is a ubiquitous organism that is classified as a fungus but shares biologic characteristics with protozoa.
Jiroveci refers to the distinct species that infects humans.
Pneumocystis jiroveci infections are actively acquired from the environment or humans.
Mode of transmission in humans is unknown, although respiratory route is most likely.

May cause infection in normal hosts as early as 2 years of age but rarely causes symptoms in immunocompetent hosts; two thirds of healthy children have antibodies to Pneumocystis jiroveci by age 2 to 4 years.
Most of the recurrences are due to new infection rather than activation of latent prior infecton.
PCP may cause a characteristic intraalveolar acellular eosinophilic exudate that can fill the alveoli.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Immunosuppressive therapy including corticosteroids for more than 1 month, vincristine, infliximab and low lymphocyte count.

list.listitem: Guidelines from the Center for Disease Control (CDC), National Institutes of Health, and the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America emphasize the importance of antiretroviral therapy for the prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections.

Chemoprophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is recommended for patients with HIV and CD4 counts <100 cells/µL regardless of plasma HIV levels or those with CD4 counts 100-200 cells/µL with plasma HIV RNA levels above detection limits. One double-strength tablet daily is the preferred regimen but one single-strength tablet daily also is effective and might be better tolerated. A

For chemoprophylaxis, dapsone, atovaquone, and aerosolized pentamidine are alternatives for those who cannot tolerate trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with consideration of Toxoplasma gondii prevention guiding the choice of these alternatice agents.

Primary prophylaxis for PCP should be discontinued when CD4 counts are higher than 200 cells/µL for more than 3 months in response to antiretroviral therapy (ART). A Primary prophylaxis for PCP may also be discontinued when CD4 count is 100–200 cells/µL and HIV RNA is undetectable for ≥3 to 6 months. B
Secondary prophylaxis should also be discontinued if CD4 counts have stayed higher than 200 cells/µL for more than 3 months as a consequence of ART. B
Prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is highly effective in immunocompromised patients without HIV.

Prophylaxis is also recommended for patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia while undergoing active treatment, and for patients receiving allogenic stem cell, hematopoietic cell or solid organ transplant. Patients with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated (ANCA) vasculitis who are undergoing induction therapy should also receive prophylaxis.

Prophylaxis against PJP should also be considered for patients receiving rituximab. In a retrospective cohort study, 1001 received PJP prophylaxis and 2523 did not. The incidence of PJP was significantly lower in the prophylaxis group (adjusted odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.42). They estimate a number needed to prevent one infection of 32 (95% CI 25 to 39).
History and physical exam are useful to differentiate PCP from other causes of pulmonary infections. C
CXR is the preferred initial imaging study.
In addition to CXR, consider measuring arterial blood gas and serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels to support diagnosis and determine severity. C
A definitive diagnosis of PCP requires identification of Pneumocystis jiroveci organism in tissue, induced sputum or BAL specimen. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Acute onset, increased incidence in all HIV patients
Typically cavitary lesions on CXR; should have a high index of suspicion
Travel history, history of soil disruption, and serology are useful
Travel history and serology are useful
Occupational history, connective tissue disease history, and bronchoscopy are useful
In HIV and non-HIV populations, CXR changes similar to those of PCP
Prior history of congestive heart failure or diastolic dysfunction

list.listitem: Patients may present with subacute onset of progressive dyspnea, a nonproductive cough or cough productive of clear sputum, malaise, and a low-grade fever.
However, the presence or absence of these symptoms does not help in ruling out other causes of pulmonary disease.
Combination of exertional dyspnea with infiltrate, low O2 saturation, thrush, or clear sputum are all specific for PCP (LR+ 4.0-7.3).
The most common manifestations of PCP among persons with HIV are the subacute onset of progressive dyspnea, fever, nonproductive cough, and chest discomfort that worsens within days to weeks.

Sputum induction with cytochemical or immunofluorescent staining is the most rapid and least invasive method of diagnosis. Immunofluorescent staining has a higher sensitivity compared with cytochemical staining.
Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with BAL is the usual gold standard test, with sensitivity greater than 90%, and should be performed if induced sputum is negative.

Stained samples of respiratory tract fluid/tissue have the following relative diagnostic sensitivities: <50% to >90% for induced sputum, 90% to 99% for bronchoscopy with BAL, 95% to 100% for transbronchial biopsy, and 95% to 100% for open lung biopsy.
Serum beta-D-Glucan (one of the major components of the cyst wall of PCP) has high sensitivity but low specificity.
Serum LDH is not diagnostic (good sensitivity but poor specificity) but has some prognostic significance.
An alveolar arterial gradient (A-a gradient) greater than 45 and diminished diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO) help in assessing the severity of PCP.
CXR is the preferred initial imaging study. In one study of 103 patients, 78 had an interstitial pattern, 13 an alveolar pattern, and 13 both.
When CXR is nondiagnostic, high-resolution CT is recommended. It is very sensitive and shows patchy or nodular ground-glass opacities.
PCR of BAL specimen is highly sensitive but cannot distinguish colonization from active disease; samples from induced sputum or oropharyngeal wash are less sensitive.
Lung biopsy is very rarely needed.
See algorithm in .
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the treatment of choice for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. A
Oral outpatient therapy is highly effective in patients with mild to moderate disease. A

Patients with HIV, documented PCP, and moderate to severe disease as defined by PaO2 <70 mm Hg or A-a gradient >35 mm Hg should receive corticosteroids within 72 hours after starting specific PCP therapy. A
HIV antiretroviral therapy should be started within 2 weeks of initial diagnosis of PCP. A
Treatment for PCP should be initiated before making a definitive diagnosis, because organisms persist in clinical specimens for days or weeks after effective therapy is initiated.

For treatment, one of the following antibiotics may be used with or without steroids: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (first line), clindamycin and primaquine, IV pentamidine, atovaquone suspension (less effective but fewer side effects than TMP-SMX) or TMP with dapsone. Patients may be treated with oral or IV antibiotics depending on the severity. Treatment is recommended for 21 days. Standard doses are trimethoprim (15-20 mg/kg) and sulfamethoxazole (75-100 mg/kg) intravenously (IV) or by mouth daily in four divided doses.

For patients with mild to moderate PCP, the rates of dose-limiting toxicity, therapeutic failure, and survival did not differ among patients who were receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin and primaquine, or dapsone with trimethoprim in a randomized, double blind study.
Another study demonstrated similar efficacy of clindamycin/primaquine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (success rate 76% vs. 79%, respectively) in patients with mild to moderate PJP.

Use of adjunctive corticosteroids is encouraged in HIV patients with PCP who have an A-a gradient greater than 35 or PaO2 less than 70. Steroids do not increase the risk of developing tuberculosis or other HIV-related disease. The NNT to prevent one death is between 9 and 23 (depending on the absence or presence of simultaneous ART therapy). The preferred corticosteroid dose and regimen is prednisone 40 mg twice daily for 1 to 5 days, then 40 mg daily for days 6 to 10 and 20 mg daily for days 11 to 21.
Immunocompromized patients without HIV who had severe PCP did not have a reduction in 28 day mortality with the addition of corticosteroids in a randomised controlled trial.

Treatment failure (determined after 4-8 days of anti-PCP treatment) occurs in approximately 10% of patients with mild-moderate disease; parenteral pentamidine or primaquine combined with clindamycin are commonly used.

In a systematic review of second-line treatment for patients with AIDS who fail trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin-primaquine had a better response rate (73%) compared with intravenous pentamidine (44%); however, no prospective RCT have evaluated an optimal approach.
Secondary prophylaxis for PCP should be continued after 21 days of treatment for PCP.
Patients with moderate to severe disease who cannot tolerate oral medications and patients with hypoxemia and tachypnea should be hospitalized.
Patients with severe PCP should be offered ICU admission or mechanical ventilation when appropriate (e.g., when they have reasonable functional status).
Complications of PCP can be due to medication side effects or the disease effects. Respiratory failure and pneumothorax are the major complications.
Risk factors for pneumothorax include a previous episode of pneumocystosis, the use of aerosol pentamidine, and cigarette smoking.
It is important to wait at least 4 to 8 days before switching therapy due to lack of clinical improvement. B
Followup after therapy includes assessment for early relapse and initiation of PCP prophylaxis until CD4 counts are higher than 200 cells/µL for at least 3 months. B
Factors associated with a worse outcome include elevated white blood cell count, elevated serum LDH, multiple admissions, decreased PaO2 and PaCO2, and decreased serum albumin.
Early readmission is more likely in patients who left the hospital against medical advice, lived in poorer, urban neighborhoods, were hospitalized in the summer, or had a recent previous admission.

In a study of patients without HIV with PCP, factors associated with acute respiratory failure included intubation delay, longer duration of PCP, and pneumothorax. The severity of CXR abnormalities was directly associated with prognosis in patients without HIV with PCP: 0/18 with early stage disease, 14/50 with mid-stage disease, and 22/37 with severe disease on CXR.Mortality is higher (30%-50%) for persons without HIV, with poorer prognosis seen in those with high A-a gradient, combined bacteremia, increased BUN and preexisting lung disease.
Early and reversible deterioration is typical in the first 3 to 5 days of therapy, probably because of the inflammatory response caused by antibiotic induced lysis of organisms in the lung.
Possible complications are respiratory failure, pneumothorax, and extrapulmonary manifestations.
Monitor for adverse effects of anti-PCP therapy.
Patients should adhere to ART to prevent resistance and maintain high CD4 counts.
Diagnosis and indications for therapy are the same as for nonpregnant women.

The preferred initial therapy for treatment and prevention during pregnancy is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Other alternative therapies, such as aerosolized pentamidine or oral atovaquone, can be considered for prevention in the first trimester based on theoretical concerns about possible teratogenicity.
Adjunctive corticosteroids should be used for the same indications as in nonpregnant women.

PCP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indicated for newborns born to mothers with HIV until their HIV status is known or for the first year of life, after which CD4 cell count may be used to guide prophylaxis.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the recommended treatment for PCP. Pentamidine can be used in children intolerant of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or who have treatment failure with it. Data are limited for the use of other alternative therapies in children.

PCP prophylaxis can be discontinued for children with HIV who are ≥6 years on ART for ≥6 months when CD4 percentage is ≥15% or CD4 count is ≥200 cells/μL. PCP prophylaxis can be discontinued for children 1 to 6 years old on ART when CD4 percentage is ≥15% or CD4 count is ≥500 cells/μL for >3 consecutive months.

cell.label: Clinical suspicion for PCP infection by history and physical exam Consider pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas (ABG).

If still high index of suspicion for PCP, perform high-resolution CT. If changes consistent with PCP are present (bilateral ground glass opacities or mosaic pattern), start treatment and confirm diagnosis.
Confirm diagnosis with sputum induction for immunofluorescent staining.
Do bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with or without PCR assay.
Look for other etiologies, consider treatment for atypical pneumonia or observation if patient is stable.
If patient is sick and clinical suspicion is high, start empiric therapy. Add steroids if PAO2 <70 mm Hg on room air.
